content:
# Keeping a Human in the Loop: Nine Tools for Supervising Coding Agents

A year ago the hard part of agentic coding was getting an agent to produce something useful. In 2026 the hard part is deciding what it is allowed to do without asking. Agents run longer, touch more files, and hit more moments where a person should decide. The tools below are all responses to that shift, and they split roughly into two groups: interfaces that put the decision in front of you, and processes that decide which decisions are worth your time.

## The bottleneck moved to approval

An agent that finishes in thirty seconds can be watched in a terminal. An agent that runs for forty minutes cannot. Once runs get long, three things break at once: you stop seeing when the agent needs you, the request arrives without the context you need to judge it, and there is no record of what you approved.

Most of the tools here fix one of those three. The interesting ones fix two.

## Answer from your phone

[[link:/tools/1648|Pocketty]] is an SSH terminal for iPhone and iPad built for exactly this moment. It alerts your phone the instant an agent is blocked or finished, sealed so that only that phone can read the alert, and then opens the exact pane over SSH so you can answer with real keystrokes rather than a chat proxy. You can swipe in for the diff of the current turn and preview dev-server ports from the same screen. It is a paid app after a fourteen-day trial, and it assumes a pane-based workflow, but it is the most direct answer to "my agent is waiting and I am not at my desk."

## A review inbox instead of a wall of text

[[link:/tools/1651|Pinrail]] is a desktop app where coding agents ask before they act. The design decision that makes it work is that the agent decides which steps need a person, so you are not approving everything. The second is that each request gets a view built for its content: a code review shows the diff with the agent findings on it, while a set of generated images can be marked up directly.

It works with any agent that can run a command, which covers Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode, and it is Apache-2.0 with a separate plugin repository. It is in early development and Windows support is still listed as coming.

## Every agent as a contact

[[link:/tools/1654|littleguys]] takes a different approach to the same problem: it turns each coding agent into a chat contact in a Mac menu-bar app. Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Goose, OpenCode and any ACP-compliant agent all appear as contacts, and commands that need approval show up as cards you can allow once, always allow or deny.

Because it speaks the Agent Client Protocol, new agents are one click away from the ACP registry. It is free and open source, requires macOS 13 or later, and it finds gateways on your tailnet and LAN by itself. The obvious caution is that it holds gateway tokens and approves real commands on your machines.

## One board for every lane

[[link:/tools/1659|Weatherdeck]] is a read-only status board for the machines and the work running on them. Small pushers feed a television or phone page showing what is waiting on you, how long it has waited, a named plate and state for each machine, and a running log. It ships a demo mode with invented sources so you can see what it looks like before wiring anything up. It is explicitly not a monitoring or alerting system, which is a useful thing for a tool to admit about itself.

## Agents that share notes

Running two agents on the same branch usually means copying context between them by hand. [[link:/tools/1650|Jotbus]] gives them a shared, end-to-end encrypted scratchpad. It registers with each agent you pick and adds a hook so @mentions reach them, which means an agent on your laptop can ask an agent on your desktop to review a change independently.

It is instant to try with no signup, workspaces are encrypted and short-lived by design, and the client states plainly that it never reads your code, history or credentials. The setup does write to your agent configuration files, so it is worth reading what it changes before you run it.

## A shared workspace for a team

[[link:/tools/1656|Agor]] scales the same idea to a team. It runs Claude Code, Codex, Gemini and others on isolated git branches, each with its own dev environment and conversation history, and presents them on live spatial boards where colleagues can watch the work and reuse what already worked. Agents carry memory, skills and tool connections, so what one person figures out is available to everyone. It installs with npm; note that the license is business source rather than OSI open source.

## Making the agent stop performing

Not every supervision problem is about approval. [[link:/tools/1652|terse]] is a Claude Code plugin aimed at a different annoyance: replies that arrive as essays, full of slogans, metaphors and it-is-not-X-it-is-Y constructions. It installs as a plugin rather than a system prompt, which is what makes it survive past a few turns, and the author reports 46 percent fewer words and 51 percent lower cost on Fable 5.1.

## Process, not hope

The two process tools here solve the upstream question: which steps deserve a person at all. [[link:/tools/1647|AI-DLC]] from AWS Labs turns coding assistants into structured delivery workflows through one harness-neutral core that runs in Claude Code, Kiro, Codex CLI, Cursor, opencode and GitHub Copilot, installed via a native command.

[[link:/tools/1653|BlastLoop]] is a lighter-weight version of the same instinct. Work is written at three altitudes named Blast, Mid and Inner, each with an owner, and results then pass T1 structural, T2 bug and ops, and T3 adversarial gates in a fixed order. You can start using it by pointing an agent at the repository's AGENTS.md file.

## How to choose

If your problem is that you are away from the machine when the agent blocks, start with Pocketty. If your problem is that approvals arrive without context, start with Pinrail. If you run more than two agents at once, littleguys or Agor will pay for themselves quickly. And if you cannot yet articulate which steps need a human, that is the problem AI-DLC and BlastLoop are built to solve, and it is worth solving before buying any of the interfaces above.
